cards.definition: A metal containing iron, such as steel and cast iron; generally magnetic and prone to rusting.
A metal that does not contain iron, such as aluminium, copper and brass; generally resistant to corrosion.
A mixture of two or more elements, at least one of which is a metal, to improve properties; e.g. steel (iron + carbon).
A plastic that can be repeatedly heated and reshaped; examples include PET, ABS, acrylic and nylon.
A plastic that sets permanently when heated and cannot be reshaped; examples include melamine, epoxy resin and urea formaldehyde.
Timber from broad-leaved, deciduous trees, e.g. oak, mahogany and beech; generally denser and slower growing than softwood.
Timber from coniferous, evergreen trees, e.g. pine, spruce and fir; generally less dense and faster growing than hardwood.
A material made from two or more constituent materials with different properties, e.g. glass-reinforced plastic (GRP) or MDF.
A material that responds to changes in its environment, such as thermochromic ink (changes colour with temperature) or shape memory alloy.
A material developed through new technologies, such as graphene, Kevlar or conductive thread, offering enhanced performance.
The maximum stress a material can withstand when being stretched or pulled before breaking.
The ability of a material to withstand forces that push or compress it without breaking or deforming.
A material's ability to resist scratching, indentation or wear.
The ability of a material to be hammered, pressed or rolled into shape without cracking.
The ability of a material to be drawn out into a wire or thread without breaking.
A material's ability to absorb energy and resist fracturing when subjected to impact or shock forces.
The ability of a material to return to its original shape after a deforming force is removed.
The ability of a material to transfer heat; metals are good thermal conductors, wood and plastics are insulators.
The ability of a material to carry an electric current; copper and aluminium are good conductors, plastics are insulators.
Mass per unit volume; a key property when selecting materials for lightweight or load-bearing applications.
Textile fibres obtained from plants or animals, e.g. cotton (plant), wool and silk (animal).
Textile fibres made from chemical processes, typically derived from petrochemicals, e.g. polyester, nylon and acrylic.
Fabric produced by interlacing warp and weft threads at right angles on a loom; durable and relatively non-stretch.
Fabric produced by interlocking loops of yarn; stretchy and comfortable, used in clothing and sportswear.
Fabric made by bonding fibres together by heat, pressure or adhesive rather than weaving; e.g. felt and interfacing.
Treatment applied to a metal surface to protect or decorate it, e.g. painting, galvanising, anodising or electroplating.
Treatment applied to protect or enhance wood, e.g. varnish, lacquer, wax, paint or oil.
The process of drying wood to reduce its moisture content before use, preventing warping and splitting.
Bonding layers of material together to improve strength or appearance, e.g. laminated timber beams or laminated plastics.
Individual parts used to build electronic circuits, including resistors, capacitors, diodes, transistors and LEDs.
A short statement that outlines the problem a designer must solve and the purpose of the product to be designed.
A detailed list of criteria that the final product must meet, covering function, size, materials, cost and target user.
A cyclical process of designing, prototyping, testing and refining, repeating the cycle until the best solution is reached.
Designing products to fit the human body and its capabilities, making them comfortable, safe and efficient to use.
Data about human body dimensions and proportions used to ensure products are the right size for the intended user.
A design approach that keeps the needs, wants and limitations of the end user at the centre of every design decision.
An early model or sample of a product built to test and evaluate a design concept before full production.
Creating a physical or digital representation of a design to test ideas, proportions and functionality before manufacture.
Using software to create, modify, analyse and optimise a design; allows accurate 2D drawings and 3D models.
A visual collage of images, colours, textures and materials used to communicate the aesthetic direction of a design.
Gathering information about the needs and preferences of potential customers to inform product design decisions.
Original data collected first-hand by the designer through methods such as surveys, interviews and observations.
Data gathered from existing sources such as books, websites and reports, rather than collected directly by the designer.
The specific group of people a product is designed for, defined by characteristics such as age, lifestyle and income.
Relating to the visual appearance and style of a product; how it looks and whether it appeals to the target user.
What a product is designed to do; a primary criterion in any design specification.
Testing and assessing a product against the design specification to identify how well it meets its criteria.
Designing products so they can be produced efficiently, cost-effectively and with minimal waste.
Legal protection for creative work, including patents (inventions), trademarks (brands) and copyright (artistic works).
Official standards produced by the British Standards Institution (BSI) to ensure products are safe, reliable and fit for purpose.
A manufacturing method that involves removing material from a workpiece, e.g. cutting, drilling, filing and turning.
A manufacturing method that reshapes material without removing it, e.g. bending, pressing, casting and forging.
A manufacturing method that builds up a product by adding material, e.g. 3D printing and welding.
A process where liquid material (e.g. molten metal) is poured into a mould and allowed to solidify into shape.
A process where molten plastic is injected under pressure into a mould and cooled to produce a component; used for high-volume production.
A process where a sheet of thermoplastic is heated until soft and then drawn over a mould using suction.
A process used to produce hollow plastic items by inflating a heated plastic tube inside a mould, e.g. bottles.
A process where material is pushed through a shaped die to produce a continuous length of a fixed cross-section, e.g. plastic pipes.
A CNC process that uses a focused laser beam to cut or engrave materials; accurate and suitable for prototyping and production.
Fused Deposition Modelling; an additive manufacturing process that builds objects layer by layer from a thermoplastic filament.
Computer Numerical Control — automated machine tools controlled by computer programs to cut, drill or shape materials accurately.
A machining process that uses a rotating cutter to remove material from a workpiece to produce complex shapes and flat surfaces.
A machining process where a workpiece is rotated while a cutting tool removes material to produce cylindrical shapes.
Creating holes in a material using a rotating drill bit; the most common manufacturing operation.
Joining metal components by melting the materials at the joint, usually with a filler metal, to form a strong bond.
Joining metal components using a lower-melting-point filler (solder) without melting the base metal; used in electronics.
Joining metals using a brass-based filler metal at a higher temperature than soldering but lower than welding.
Joining materials using glue or adhesive; types include PVA (wood), epoxy resin (metals/plastics) and contact adhesives.
Joining components using screws, nuts and bolts, rivets or snap-fits — methods that are often non-permanent and allow disassembly.
Checking products during and after manufacture against specifications to ensure they meet required standards, using gauges and inspection.
Manufacturing a single, unique item to a customer's specification; highly skilled and expensive, e.g. bespoke furniture.
Making a specific quantity of identical products in one run before switching to a different product; flexible and cost-effective.
Manufacturing large quantities of the same product continuously using automated machinery; low unit cost but inflexible.
Non-stop manufacturing of the same product 24/7, e.g. steel rolling or paper making; used for commodities.
A device that holds a workpiece in place and guides a cutting tool to ensure accurate and repeatable operations.
A pattern or shape used to mark out or check a component to ensure accurate replication.
The acceptable variation in the size of a manufactured component above or below a stated dimension.
Using computer software to control manufacturing machinery, e.g. CNC routers, laser cutters and 3D printers.
Designing a product with a deliberately limited lifespan to encourage consumers to buy replacements.
A production philosophy that aims to minimise waste (time, materials and effort) while maximising value and efficiency.
A set of connected parts that work together to perform a function; described using input, process and output.
A signal or component that provides data or energy into a system, e.g. a switch, sensor or microphone.
The part of a system that receives the input signal and performs an operation on it, e.g. a microcontroller or timer.
The result or action produced by a system, e.g. a light, buzzer, motor or display.
A component that limits the flow of electric current in a circuit; measured in ohms (Ω).
A component that stores electrical charge and releases it; used for smoothing, timing and filtering in circuits.
A semiconductor device that emits light when current flows through it in the correct direction.
A semiconductor device used to amplify or switch electronic signals; fundamental to modern electronics.
A small computer on a single chip that can be programmed to control inputs and outputs; e.g. Arduino.
An electronic input device that detects changes in the environment (light, temperature, sound) and converts them to electrical signals.
V = IR; the voltage across a component equals the current through it multiplied by its resistance.
A circuit in which components are connected one after another in a single path; current is the same throughout.
A circuit in which components are connected across the same two points; voltage is the same across each branch.
A board that mechanically supports and electrically connects electronic components using conductive tracks.
An electronic switch that performs a logical operation (AND, OR, NOT) on one or more binary inputs to produce an output.
Using information from the output of a system to adjust the input and improve or stabilise the system's performance.
An electronic component that can be programmed to perform specific tasks, such as a microcontroller or PIC chip.
A device that converts an electrical signal into a physical action, such as a motor, solenoid or servo.
A circuit using two resistors in series to produce an output voltage that is a fraction of the input voltage.
A network of physical devices embedded with sensors and software that connect and exchange data over the internet.
Designing products that minimise environmental impact throughout their lifecycle, from material extraction to disposal.
An evaluation of the environmental impact of a product at every stage of its life: extraction, manufacture, use and disposal.
A framework for sustainable design: Reduce, Reuse, Recycle, Rethink, Refuse and Repair.
The total amount of greenhouse gases produced during the manufacture, transport, use and disposal of a product.
Natural resources that exist in limited quantities and cannot be replaced once used, e.g. oil, coal and metal ores.
Materials or energy sources that are naturally replenished, e.g. timber from managed forests and solar energy.
A trading system ensuring workers in developing countries receive fair wages and safe conditions for producing goods.
Designing products so components can be easily separated at end-of-life for reuse, recycling or safe disposal.
An economic model designed to eliminate waste by keeping materials in use as long as possible through reuse and recycling.
Intentionally designing products to become outdated or fail after a set period, driving repeat purchases at an environmental cost.
Considerations about the impact of design and manufacturing on people, communities and values, e.g. exploitation of workers or cultural sensitivity.
Designing products usable by as many people as possible regardless of age, disability or other factors.
The process by which businesses and products operate internationally; enables cheaper production but may exploit low-wage economies.
How the traditions, values and aesthetics of different cultures shape the style and function of designed products.
Laws and standards that designers and manufacturers must comply with, e.g. CE marking, REACH regulations and the Health & Safety at Work Act.
Requirements that products must meet to be considered safe for sale and use, enforced by bodies such as the BSI and Trading Standards.
International symbols on packaging and products indicating the material type and whether it is recyclable.
Transforming waste materials or old products into something of higher quality or value rather than simply recycling.
A model that considers all impacts of a product from raw material extraction ('cradle') to disposal ('grave').
A design philosophy where all materials are cycled back safely into the environment or industry at end-of-life, eliminating waste.
